coverage: Seven chapters absent from the previous 43-reference Scripture sample because they chiefly develop theology, history, prayer or discipline rather than an individually printed Bible verse. This is not a claim those chapters have no Bible citations.

entries.title: Liturgical Latin: unity, stability, and historical limits
entries.claimEn: Lanslots treats Latin as a stable common language through which worshippers from many nations are joined in the Roman rite. His argument belongs to the historical and pastoral explanation of Latin; it is not a proof that the Roman Mass was celebrated exclusively in Latin from apostolic times.
entries.claimFr: Le latin sert de langue liturgique commune et stable dans le rite romain. Cet usage exprime l’unité de la prière de l’Église, mais l’histoire des langues liturgiques ne se réduit pas à une continuité exclusivement latine depuis les Apôtres.
entries.reviewNote: Author's statement at OCR 1650 that Mass had been offered in Latin 'from the time of the apostles' is historically unsafe; he also correctly acknowledges Eastern liturgical languages at OCR 1620–1630. Historical chronology needs original scholarship; no normative 1962 rubric is inferred.

entries.title: Psalm 42 and penitence at the altar's foot
entries.claimEn: The approach to the altar joins the Sign of the Cross, the desire to draw near to God, Psalm 42 and the acknowledgment of sin. Lanslots insists that outward details do not all require mystical interpretations; the rites direct worshippers toward the Sacrifice rather than invite arbitrary symbolism.
entries.claimFr: Au pied de l’autel, le signe de croix, le psaume Judica et l’aveu des fautes disposent à s’approcher de Dieu. La signification spirituelle des prières ne permet pas pour autant d’inventer une allégorie pour chaque détail pratique.
entries.reviewNote: The author's assertion that all present kneel (OCR 1854–1857) is a period custom, not universal 1962 posture law; the omission of Psalm 42 is controlled separately for current 1962 forms.

entries.title: Creed and the Incarnation
entries.claimEn: The Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed professes the divinity of the Son, the Incarnation, the saving Passion, and the Church's faith. The gesture at Et incarnatus est expresses reverence for the true taking of human nature by the eternal Word; its exact performance belongs to the approved rubrics.
entries.claimFr: Le Credo professe la divinité du Fils et le mystère de l’Incarnation : le Verbe a réellement assumé notre nature humaine. L’agenouillement au passage Et incarnatus est signifie l’adoration de ce mystère; sa réalisation exacte dépend des rubriques applicables.
entries.reviewNote: Author's 1897 feast list for saying the Creed (OCR 3027–3053) is not the 1962 prescription. His historical description of the development of the Creed (OCR 3055–3098) requires critical chronology review; no unsourced fabricated Scripture verse is attached.

entries.title: Silence and ecclesial sacrifice in Te igitur
entries.claimEn: The priest begins the Canon by praying for the Church and offering sacrifice to the Father through Christ. Its quiet recitation demands interior attention, not disengagement: the prayer remains a liturgical act while the faithful join its intention and adoration.
entries.claimFr: Au Te igitur, le prêtre adresse au Père, par le Christ, la supplication et l’offrande de l’Église. Le silence du Canon n’est pas une absence d’action : il appelle au recueillement et à l’union intérieure au Sacrifice.
entries.reviewNote: Author calls Canon language a special inspiration of Holy Ghost (OCR 4930–4934); distinguish non-biblical liturgical composition from inspired canonical Scripture. The 'ordination Mass' example at OCR 4940–4948 is 1897 historically situated, not current role instruction.

entries.title: Memento of the living and Communicantes
entries.claimEn: The Memento of the Living remembers particular persons within the Church's offering, while the Communicantes expresses communion with the saints in heavenly glory. These are two different movements of intercession within the one Canon.
entries.claimFr: Le Mémento des vivants présente à Dieu les personnes pour lesquelles l’Église prie. Le Communicantes unit cette prière à la communion de la Vierge Marie, des apôtres et des saints : les deux supplications ont leur place propre dans l’unique Canon.
entries.reviewNote: The author's old Communicantes list omits St Joseph, who appears in the 1962 Canon; hagiographical narratives later in this chapter mix legendary and historical material, requiring individual primary witness and no automatic import to saints library.

entries.title: Memento of the dead and Nobis quoque peccatoribus
entries.claimEn: The Church offers the Eucharistic Sacrifice while asking repose, light and peace for the departed. Nobis quoque then turns the supplication toward the sinners still on earth, asking fellowship with the saints through divine mercy rather than personal merit.
entries.claimFr: Au Mémento des défunts, l’Église demande pour eux le repos, la lumière et la paix en offrant le Saint Sacrifice. Puis, au Nobis quoque, elle implore pour nous, pécheurs, une place parmi les saints, non selon nos mérites, mais par la miséricorde divine.
entries.reviewNote: Author's statements about exclusion from named intercession and Mass intentions (OCR 7260–7314) reflect a 19th-century ecclesiastical discussion and may be overstated; they do NOT define universal contemporary funeral, private prayer, or 1962 rubric permissions. Avoid prose implying physical blood runs into purgatory.

entries.title: Per ipsum, the minor elevation, and Pater noster
entries.claimEn: Per ipsum offers all honour and glory to the Father through, with and in Christ. The minor elevation belongs to this doxology. The Lord's Prayer then joins praise of the Father to the petition for daily bread and prepares the way for Communion.
entries.claimFr: Le Per ipsum rend au Père toute gloire par le Christ, avec lui et en lui; la petite élévation accompagne cette doxologie. Le Pater noster tourne ensuite l’assemblée vers le Père, demande le pain quotidien et prépare la communion.
entries.reviewNote: Historical explanation of blessing food and original Mass frequency (OCR 7720–7759) needs independent historical corroboration. Canon finishes within AO.CANON.14 at B061; Pater starts next current base macro at B062. Exact action cues belong to canonical 1962 sources.

invariants: Bilingual paragraphs are research-only paraphrase drafts; they must not be silently activated as Guide text.
No adoption of nineteenth-century historical/pastoral generalizations as 1962 rules.
Canon sections derive from current source-first Canon map, not inferred 48-card historical positions.
Scripture citations must be explicit, or marked editorially mapped. Missing biblical verse is not automatically a problem for theological/historical paragraphs.
